meta.storyTitle: Remove the existing daemon installer and lifecycle implementation
meta.triageRationale: One cohesive, deliberately scoped removal, not a new subsystem or multiple independent capabilities. A single standalone design must coordinate deletion and retained behavior across backend, scripts and both IDE clients. The 278-file/176-member manifests make much of the removal mechanical, but broad live callers and shared transport/keystore/resource closure boundaries require multiple build tasks and explicit design; small/trivial would understate impact.

summary.prose: Remove the existing daemon installer, upgrade, supervisor and start/stop implementation so a replacement can be designed from a clean baseline. Delete the 278 dedicated files and the 176 identified member/test slices, and remove their client, build and release wiring. Preserve shared application behavior and retained test assertions; this change does not install a replacement engine or operate the running daemon.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

boundary.internal: Remove the existing daemon installer and lifecycle implementation

dataModelChanges.entity: Existing daemon installation and process-control surface
dataModelChanges.details: Remove the whole-file and member contracts enumerated in the two committed manifests, including lifecycle-only result/types/fields, update acknowledgement hooks, PID/selection/controller ownership, CLI and IDE controls, native helpers and release authority. Exact accounting is 278 whole files (143 implementation/build/asset/CI,115 tests,20 helpers) and176 member/test entries in70 other files. No new public API or persistent schema is introduced. Removed IPC methods use existing generic unsupported/method-not-found handling; lifecycle controls disappear from CLI/IDE surfaces. Do not retain compatibility facades or silently route to old files.

dataModelChanges.entity: Retained application, transport and shared guard ownership
dataModelChanges.details: After removal, CLI/IDE consumers continue to use generic IPC one-to-one request channels for remaining methods; no control-engine dependency remains. Shared process identity and keystore guard acquisition/conflict/reclamation remain owned by shared code, with multiple consumers preserved. Resource-close callbacks stay application-owned: store/worker/queue/socket flush and cleanup must remain coherent without the old supervisor/watchdog/transaction authority. Preserve model/configuration bootstrap, workflow artifact approvals, backups/compaction/status, host/MCP registration and generic launch contracts. Remove only lifecycle execution slices from mixed routines. Existing installed user state has no ownership transfer and no migration; it is untouched.

errorCases.scenario: A candidate file or member source no longer matches the committed snapshot.
errorCases.detection: Manifest path/hash and member-selector checks fail before editing, or a current caller scan finds a new preservation obligation.
errorCases.response: Stop the affected deletion batch, reconcile that record with current source, and report the concrete change. Never blindly delete by stale line ranges.
errorCases.userImpact: Cleanup pauses for correction; unrelated source and installed user state stay intact.

errorCases.scenario: Removal leaves an unresolved import, registered command, resource asset or test selector.
errorCases.detection: Current-source reference scan, TypeScript/client build, packaging input check or focused retained test fails.
errorCases.response: Remove the exclusively lifecycle registration or rewire the retained contract at its existing boundary, then rerun the affected check. Do not restore the retired engine or disable broad checks to make the build pass.
errorCases.userImpact: Branch is incomplete until the integration check passes.

errorCases.scenario: A shared guard, model/configuration, workflow or resource-close invariant is accidentally removed.
errorCases.detection: Retained boundary tests or compiler use-sites fail; manifest accounting shows a mixed-test/function range was removed wholesale.
errorCases.response: Restore the preserved behavior from baseline, narrow the lifecycle slice and revalidate that boundary.
errorCases.userImpact: Prevents collateral loss of application functionality.

edgeCases.input: A previously installed client sends a removed lifecycle IPC method.
edgeCases.expected: Existing generic method-not-found handling; no update, stop, fallback shell invocation or ambient runtime probing.

edgeCases.input: An existing external daemon or retained user installation remains running during source cleanup.
edgeCases.expected: No process, launch job, socket, installed tree, journal, trust record or store outside the workspace is altered.

edgeCases.input: A mixed model/configuration flow previously executed a daemon restart.
edgeCases.expected: Remove that execution and old restart-control UI; preserve saved model/configuration decisions, no-duplicate-approval behavior and truthful apply-later information.

edgeCases.input: Resource-close expectations reside in a test that also asserts old watchdog/ownership mechanics.
edgeCases.expected: Replace only the old lifecycle assertions; preserve the actual resource drain/close contract.

invariantsToPreserve.text: Generic IPC transport remains available to the broad application/IDE/configuration/approval consumers; only lifecycle-specific methods/hooks are removed.
Shared process identity and keystore guard acquisition, conflict and reclamation survive removal of lifecycle-only guard transfer/borrowing.
Removal accounting follows the exact committed file/member scope; retained behavior in mixed sources and tests is preserved and no installed state is mutated.

testStrategy.testFramework: Use the repository's existing Node test coordinator and TypeScript test conventions, VS Code test/bundle scripts and JetBrains focused JUnit/Gradle bridge. Preserve test-harness process ownership and bounds. Tests are run only after all relevant code tasks have been built, with one story build approval after final validation rather than per task.

migration.stateBefore: As grounded in s1 c1/c2, the branch contains the existing macOS managed/legacy, Linux source, owned-runtime, release and client lifecycle paths; generic IPC and shared guard dependencies must survive. Both deletion manifests and evidence are committed at728c31abc; source hashes match and the working tree was clean before this tracked design.
migration.stateAfter: The old engine and its dedicated tests are absent from workspace source. Mixed-file lifecycle contracts/controls/hooks are removed with preserved generic transport, configuration/model/workflow/data behavior and application resource cleanup. Source installation/update/start/stop controls are intentionally unavailable pending a separately designed replacement. Existing installed user trees, daemon processes and stores are unchanged.

migrationSteps.action: Freeze the committed manifests and verify source hashes/selectors; prepare batch accounting and retained boundary checks.
Remove dedicated lifecycle sources, native/runtime/release assets and their dedicated tests/helpers; adjust surviving build/package/CI references.
Remove backend and CLI lifecycle member slices, retaining generic IPC/keystore guards/model bootstrap/resource-close callback bodies and other service behavior.

Remove VS Code and JetBrains lifecycle control/freshness/auto-start/installer wiring and corresponding mixed-test slices; retain status/backup/compact, model/settings and host/MCP registration behavior.
Reconcile source inventories and documentation of the temporary branch state; run one build and focused retained validation, account for all files/members and report remaining limitations.

migration.backwardCompat: Deliberate development-branch removal of old lifecycle commands and IPC contracts. No compatibility facade, hidden fallback or automatic install/upgrade migration is retained. Existing generic method-not-found behavior handles callers of removed methods; no advertised control may report success without implementation. Other application/IDE IPC contracts remain aligned. No release is published by this change.

alternativesConsidered.name: Manifest-driven deletion with retained application cleanup in place
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Delete both identified sets, remove old control APIs/UI, and retain only existing application startup/resource-close behavior in the surviving modules.
alternativesConsidered.approach: The two committed manifests own deletion accounting. Remove dedicated files and identified lifecycle slices; strip client command/IPC/update contracts and build/release dependencies. Existing generic transports, model/configuration bootstrap, shared keystore guard primitives and application-owned resource-close callbacks remain in their current modules with direct integration. No replacement installer, supervisor, transaction journal or compatibility facade is introduced. Remove lifecycle controls from product surfaces and use existing generic method-not-found behavior for removed IPC names.
pros: Smallest change that meets the removal directive and preserves required shared behavior.
Avoids a new lifecycle abstraction and leaves replacement design separate.
Manifest accounting provides a reviewable reason for every removed file or member.
cons: Resource cleanup must be carefully separated from the old orchestration inside mixed modules.
Temporary branch intentionally lacks installation/update/process-control product capabilities.

alternativesConsidered.name: Manifest-driven deletion with an application resource-close boundary
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Delete the same old implementation but extract retained resource cleanup into a narrow application-owned close boundary.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Remove the exact whole-file and member scope, then separate queue/worker/store/socket draining from OS process supervision into a narrow internal resource-close contract. Clients and public lifecycle APIs are removed as in a1; the resource-close boundary has no installer, update, supervisor, rollback, PID/kill or release responsibilities. Preserve non-lifecycle behavior and validate the extracted close behavior in focused tests.
pros: Makes the preservation boundary explicit for complex cleanup callbacks.
Can reduce coupling between future lifecycle design and application resource ownership.
cons: Introduces an extra internal boundary/file during a deletion-only change.
More API and test churn than retaining the existing callback bodies in place.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Also meets removal/preservation scope, but the new close boundary adds API/file churn and architectural decisions not needed to remove the existing engine. Use only if implementation demonstrates retained callbacks cannot remain coherent in place.
